blocks.x: Today is April 17th, 1969 and we're interviewing Sid DeVilla at the Mardi Gras Club. Is it Mardi Gras Lounge?
Mardi Gras Lounge, I guess you could call it.
Mardi Gras Lounge, 333 Berlin Street. Okay, Sid, can you tell me first of all, when you first started to run the club, what it was that first made you want to bring a jazz band in, whatever that was?

Well, I had been a musician playing around the country and playing in New Orleans for many years. Roy Zimmerman, Monk Hazel, and Leon Prima. When it was an opportunity for me to go into a business for myself, I couldn't think of anything I'd like to do better than open a club and put in the kind of music that we liked to play and enjoyed playing. And we killed two birds with one stone, I'd be the boss. Actually, I couldn't get fired that way. And no one could dictate what type of music we wanted to play.
And at the time, there were just a couple of other clubs on the street.
There were Patek Lounge and Famous Door. So we became the third club for Dixieland Music in the city, presenting Dixieland Music nightly.
Can you remember when that was? This was 1951, August 51.
And we continued that policy for a number of years, which was a happy occasion. And we made a lot of friends and employed a lot of wonderful musicians, you know?
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Well, can you tell me about how it was that you decided to hire George Lewis, the George Lewis band, and the circumstances, anything you can remember to hire him? George Lewis, yes.

There were a number of good bands around town, of which George had one. And our policy was not to keep the same band for much too long. We would change bands and alternate bands. Paul Baldwin would work a while. By a while, I mean some months. George would come in with his band, and this actually is the last spot that Papa Celestan worked a steady engagement. Two weeks after he left here is when I think he was stricken fatally and died. This is his last steady job right here, Papa Celestan. George was here at two different times, and it was a happy occasion. People thronged in the sea, and they just loved him. They were particularly fond of George, all over the world.
So, where did you, how was it that you had heard George play? Where did you heard him play before getting in here?

Records, first I heard him records. And then the Patek Lounge, which is on the other end of the block, they would bring in bands occasionally. They'd have a house band, and on the off night they would bring in a different band, another band. I guess the first time I heard George Lewis play in person was at the Patek Lounge. And I was impressed. What would be a clarinet player myself of some sort? I was impressed by his style and by his ideas and his technique. George got over the clarinet and put it on good. He was a sweetheart, he was a sweetheart. So when the opportunity presented itself, he did some off nights for us here. And then when it was time to change the band, we put George to work. And as I said, he worked two different occasions for us. Both of them were very happy occasions, incidentally.
Can you remember how long the engagements were?
George, no, I can't recall offhand, of course the contract's in the back, but I think George did about a six month stint at one time and probably another six or eight months at another time.
And what have you been playing most nights a week?

Six nights a week. Six nights a week. When he came in as a steady band, you see. And opposed to George, we had Lizzie Miles whom we resurrected. And Lizzie would do, along with Joe Robichaud, she would do the low, you know, the 15 minutes. And of course we went through many, many wonderful people like Kid Howard. We put a band together for Kid Howard and Kid was here for a while. About that time his chops came out and he had to take a respite from it. We were probably using it.
Do you remember Lizzie?
Oh yes.
Yes, I think somebody did an interview with her, I think backstage here. Back here? Yes, I think Bob Greenwood and Dick Allen.
Yeah, I think Dick was along with her.
Did an interview at some point. She was probably playing, that was about the same time George was playing here.

She was here at different times. And of course I'd let Liz go away and she'd take some engagements on the west coast. I remember one time particularly they booked her in Las Vegas. And she'd take two or three weeks off and play her engagements wherever she had to go and she'd come right back to us.

Well now tell me about the action, when the band would be playing here at night. What would be the set up? I mean how long would they play? What would be the intermission business and what sort of numbers? What would the customer reaction be and so on? How did it work out?

The band played the band again I guess about 8.30 and they did 40 or 45 minutes set which varied at different times. And the Liz and some vocalists were on Joe Rovers' show along with me, Smiling Joe. They'd fill in the low. And the band played the authentic Dixieland numbers. There was no playing the, you know, some pop request. Matter of fact there's very few people would dare request anything that wasn't on a, in a, true Dixieland style, you know. Not style so much but authentic Dixieland compositions. And the thing with Rovers' show was, oh, just the great Dixieland tunes and that these guys had more fun playing it. It seemed kind of a shame to break it up and pay them at the end of the week because they had just enjoyed their music so much, you know. They had just enjoyed it so much.
Did you have good crowds? Business was wonderful, just wonderful.

So much so that we, we contemplating getting a larger place, you know, where we could see more people, another 50 or 100 people. Because it was, just couldn't jam them in here. They would stand in the aisles and go in the back and stand outside the restroom, anywhere they could stand just to hear the band. And of course every time somebody would get up to take a solo or something, it would be pantomimony, you know. They'd show their appreciation, you know, profusely. People just loved these characters. Matter of fact is, that was the time I got to know many, many more of these jazz musicians that I hadn't known previously. Although I had been a professional, I stayed away most of my life. And I got to know just a lot, many more than I'd ever known before. And just really found out just how great they were, you know, as personal, as people, as personalities, and as musicians with a good, true musician's heart, you know.
Did you, did you ever sit in with the band? Oh yes, yes, yes. What did, how was it, how did you enjoy playing with that band?
Just great, just great. I used to sit in occasionally. Maybe once or twice on a set. Yeah. A set I'd sit in.
Of course they had a wonderful rhythm section.

Yeah, and the thing would go like a big machine. It would never stop. And it would catch you up in that and believe it, carry you along with it, whether or not you were ready to play, or you thought you were ready to play or not, you see.
Yeah. Was, uh, was Lawrence Morera playing at that time?

Lawrence was playing. I had a picture of him right here somewhere. I was just looking at him. I couldn't remember his name. Yeah, Lawrence was with the band. That's him right there, isn't it? Yeah. Is it the George Lewis band, incidentally?

Yes, that's, I've never seen that picture before. It's a very nice picture. It's, uh, got Percy Humphrey on trumpet and, uh, Yeah, Percy. Nice picture. Very nice one of Lawrence. Let's see, I wonder what, this is, studio of George Foxy. I wonder where this picture is. I don't know where it was made, tell you. I think it must have been made in New Orleans somewhere, because I don't think Percy went out of time. But that would have been in the early 50s.
I just wonder if it made in the place, because, uh, Flash, but no, it wasn't made in this place here. No, it was made somewhere else. That's, uh, who's that on bass? That wasn't slow drag.
That's slow drag, yeah.
Yeah, slow drag. And Percy. And, uh, who's on the phone, well, Robinson?
Jim Roberts.
Jim, yeah. Jim Roberts.

Jim Roberts. Well, let me ask you now about, um, um, it seems to me that in the last, I don't know, ten years, or maybe more than ten years, there's been quite a big change on Bourbon Street in terms of the kind of entertainment that's provided, and this has been presumable dictated by financial considerations and so on. Um, would you like to discuss this a little bit and the sort of change that has taken place on the street?

Well, let's see, now, first, I guess I've been on Bourbon Street about half of my life. Twenty-five years, twenty-six years altogether. And, uh, it's become more of a midway now. There's a lot of lookers and a lot of, uh, walkers, and, uh, actually the people don't go into clubs, or, and this has been the trend the last ten years, Tom. They don't go into these clubs as they used to. There'd be about sixteen girly, girly clubs, so-called strip clubs on the street. And there were three jazz places, as I mentioned, the Paddock, the Mardi Gras, and the Famous Door. Uh, and that was a whole scene on the street, not along with Pat O'Brien, you see.
Were there sixteen strip places at that time?

Mm-hmm. Sixteen. Assorted sizes, you know, and assorted operators, and assorted operations. But, uh, things change, and, uh, it's discernible now, but it was a gradual change, and, uh, we have more restaurants now. We have fewer strip clubs. We have fewer strippers. And along have come a couple of jazz places, like, uh, I think Preservation Hall and Dixieland Hall, which make an attempt at, uh, while they're not actually in the nightclub category, and they don't sell whiskey, alcohol, and, uh, there's more of a little concert effect, wouldn't you call it that? Yeah. It's a little concert effect.

And, of course, the, the, the famous store really still has jazz, and the Paddock, to a certain extent, really. I mean, they're both, they are, in a sense, both the same. Paddock Club is... Or have they changed those places?

The Paddock Club has retained their policy throughout the years. Matter of fact, I believe the Paddock was instrumental in setting the jazz reaction off on the, uh, off on the jazz trend, or what there was, off on Bourbon Street. But even before that, 1947 or 1948, uh, Leroy Primer had a club, St. Louis and Bourbon, the 500 Club. And while he presented shows, while he presented shows, he did a, the house policy was for, to have a show. And then the stage would push, push back under the bandstand, and we played for dancing. And Leon, uh, very well known Dixieland Trump, you know, I guess you know his brother, Louis Primer. And we were the first ones on the street, we were the first ones on the street, to present Dixieland tunes. And we would play our Dixieland tunes for dancing. And it was Roy Zimmerman, Monk Hazel, I think he's left us. Uh, Leon Primer and myself, and, uh, we liked the trombone, but we did the Dixieland tunes. Well, shortly after that, I think, you know, or about the time that the Paddock instituted a policy, and tried Dixieland music, and I think Pop Celestan was in there. Is that correct? About 48, 47? You had, actually had Don music for dancing, did you? We did the Dixieland music for dancing. In here?
No, no, it was at the 500 Club. Oh, this was at the 500 Club. This was before you opened your place.

About 47, 1948. So actually, that was the first, now that I know of, that was the first little Dixieland music in this area, in the French Quarter. Because prior to that, before I went to the Army in 42, there were several clubs on the street, and one in particular was the, uh, ballet club. And I had a band in there for a couple of years. But we played for dancing, and we played for shows, but we didn't make any attempt at playing Dixieland music. We played the pop music of the day, you know, for dancing, and of course we played the show numbers. But it was in the Dixieland band, and it, instrumental-wise or anything, you know, three saxophones and one guitar and one trumpet. But, uh, as I said, when I first, Leon Prem, I think opened his club shortly after the war, and he was the first one to put a taste of Dixieland on the street. So just a taste. We'd play five or six tunes, Muscat Ramble, and we'd play Saints, or we'd play, uh, Sensation, something like that. And, uh, for dancing. And then, uh, after a dance set, the show would go on. But that was the first, uh, first time I've run across Dixieland music. I actually played in the French Quarter.

Amazing. Can you remember that before, like in, uh, before the war, can you remember it at all? I mean, there was... Before the war. Or, say, around early, very early 40s, there really wasn't any, any jazz.

No, there was, there was jazz in a sense, but it was, uh, uh, currently the modern jazz. There wasn't any, uh, Dixieland. We played, uh, whatever was, uh, in the vein, all clarinet players emulated, uh, or tried to, Benny Goodman. All the saxophone players were trying to play like Vito Musso. And all the trumpet players were another Harry James. And, uh, the boys that did manage to keep this Dixieland music alive throughout all of these years, they weren't working too often, too regularly. They'd play a funeral, they'd play some socialites for dance somewhere, and, uh, and actually it was pretty thin, uh, I think George Lewis was working on the ribbon. You know?
What were the, what was the, what was it that made you change your policy here, say in the 50s or whenever it was, away from, um, a music orientation to more of, uh, entertainment?

That was a financial thing. It was, uh, kind of, uh, bumbling on my part about that. I never was a very good businessman or a bookkeeper. The fellow that I employed is a bookkeeper. He, uh, let me get the tax bind, and I had to get out in a hurry. And at the time, a very terrible thing was going on. We had to pay 20% federal excise tax, cavalry license tax. And, uh, that made deep inroads into our finances, you see. So, uh, I got myself into a stupid bind where I had to come up with some tax money right quick, and, uh, made the wrong, I had a choice of two things, taking my bands and going on the road, you see, and we had some lucrative offer. Either that or put the girls in and, uh, get this money in a hurry that way. And I chose the latter, which, to my sorrow, that I did, you know, because we had some good records out, and we had some good commitments we could have fulfilled for enough money to justify this, uh, deficit that I was faced with, you know.
So, in other words, you're saying that basically bringing the girls in is definitely a more commercial operation for me.

Oh, very much so. More commercial. And at the time, now, I'm not speaking for 1969, but 19, when we did the change, it was a quick buck. Can you remember when that was? Was a quick buck. I can't recall exactly, but let's see, we've been here 18 years, I'd say about nine, ten years ago. Yes. But we kept it as a jazz place for nine years or better.

I see. Is there any, is there much sort of, uh, do you sense that there's much sort of pressure on the street to try and perform or to produce entertainment in a certain style or anything like that? No, I don't think so. I'm always hearing, you know, you always hear these stories about the places that are being controlled by a few people and so on, and I was wondering if you had been subjected to any of these pressures or anything like that?

No, that's not, that's not true at all. These places are individually owned, and, uh, and actually, if someone would come in and, uh, not a syndicate, but an organization, which we attempted to do several times, try to, uh, put some uniformity on the street, such as prices and hours and, uh, cutthroat activities, crit to your left. I think we'd all benefit. But, uh, it's not the case. They're individually owned by guys that don't have too much money. And it's kind of a hit of scare them, catch as catch can, you know? Yes.
It's almost. Is that right? You really think that, in other words, there isn't that much uniformity on the street, do you?

No, not at all, Tom. Not at all. I've been debating putting the band back in. Matter of fact, we did, I think, 1963. We took the girls' shows out, uh, cleaned up the place a little bit, and, uh, hired a band that had worked here before, trombone player, um,
Diana Matthews, Bill Matthews. Bill came in with a wonderful band. I was a band that had worked here before, um,

Dianna Matthews. Bill Matthews. Bill came in with a wonderful band. I was looking for a picture of it back there. Kept Bill about six weeks and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and-and- catch on. Now next door, the famous door which leans on this building and if they open their side door you can hear their music in here. They've always employed white young musicians with the exception of a time or two that Santa was there and the shocking monk. But they keep a younger musician that plays a more modern style and actually it's anything but authentic Dixieland. I hate the word authentic Dixieland but I mean the phrase authentic Dixieland but it's anything but Dixieland music in the true sense. The best I can describe is the Dixieland flavored with the Dixieland instrumentation, the three front lines. But notwithstanding that their business goes on like Old Man River you know and while the rest of these places that had good music there have been times when we had some some
lean times for us you know. It's been up and down. The paddock certainly doesn't it doesn't ever strike me that it does particularly good business.

No I guess the only reason the paddock survives is because they have a get these bus tours that come on the street which is a captive audience. You buy a ticket it'll take you to so many places and if that happens to be one of them you go there whether or not you're interested you see and whether or not you really appreciate the music. But that does seem to keep about three places alive on the street the 500 Club, the show bar and the paddock. The rest of them we must take our chances as they go by or they deliberately look for us and come to see us. But before Hip died Hip owned the famous door there about 25 years or so before he passed away three or four years ago. He was bitter toward those tours that would capture these people and not let it not leave them free to walk on the street where we could all you know try to entice them into the place with music or whatnot.
How is it that you get that somebody gets the tour and somebody else doesn't?

A lot has to do with seating capacity. We first opened in 1950-51 here we got a select small limousine at the time they were called limousine tours where they would bring us 40 or 60 people or 35 or 20 people a night or at a time. But there are many times these buses pull up and you must be able to seat a couple hundred people. immediately. A couple hundred people. Because that's why they contract you for that and naturally those people have to be seated and there are only a couple of places that large on the street I believe to accommodate that. Now let me ask you when did you first start? Start? Well when I was about 12 years old. That's about 41 years ago. And were you, who, what were the influences, what were the influences, the musical influences that music that you had heard at that age? Let's see 41 and that would be 1928. About that time, yes.
It's difficult to say. We were always surrounded by jazz in New Orleans and I guess we kind of grew up with that, you know, the flavor and smell of jazz around us.

But I remember that, you know, the music that you had heard at that age, you know, the music that you had heard at that age. And I remember getting a saxophone in the clarinet and studying with Jean Parquet and Tony Parenti when I was a kid. And by George, that was about the only thing for me to do.
Whereabouts were you living at that time?
Gentilly Terrace in New Orleans.
Did you hear any of the old, some of the well-known old collared musicians of that time? No, I sure didn't.
I sure didn't. I sure didn't. I sure didn't.
I was wondering, people like Kid Rene.

No. I sure didn't. The only thing I can remember, to be truthful, because at those times people threw little parties. They had little house parties and they would hire a three or four piece band and roll back the rug in the living room, you see, and take the sofa out in the neighborhoods and they would hire a little three or four piece band and they would be dancing and near beer or a beer or a beer. Or a homebrew. But I do remember Louis Armstrong being at the suburban, suburban, suburban gardens. And he'd broadcast from there and then the late broadcast every night.
I wonder when that was, I wonder if that was the time of your time here. 31.

This was about, around the 30s. I don't know, 31. I can remember him vividly when he used to come on. Here's Louis Armstrong coming from the suburban gardens. The suburban gardens, way down in New Orleans. And they would swing and that would be it. And I'd sit there and I'd, believe me, you know, I didn't know a quarter note from all.
Well, anything else.

And, but there was something in that, that entranced me and captivated me about that music. And of course he's still today the greatest and he and I have run across each other in many cities. And the last time I saw him, he was in here listening to the band. Oh really? He was in here listening to the band.
Did you ever hear any of the parades on the streets or funerals or anything?

Always. And particularly Mardi Gras parades, you see. We didn't, of course we didn't live in the city proper, a little suburb, but we did get down from Mardi Gras on a few occasions like that. And I guess New Orleans is about to parade in the city in America. Because I've been in a lot of cities and this is a parade in the city. I don't think the people fare too well financially and economically, but if you give them a parade, it satisfies them. It makes them happy. And I guess Mardi Gras parades, ever since you were a little kid, you know, six, seven years old, you'd see the bands.

Do you think that there is much difference between the kind of Dixieland jazz that colored people play and the kind of white people playing around in your arms? Any particular time? Well, say in the twenties or thirties when you were starting, were you aware that there was any difference or do you think there's any difference now?

Well, on some instruments I could find that there's a thing that I tried to analyze was a saxophone style that came out in the warms, which was unlike any saxophone style I'd ever heard. Because I was interested in the alto saxophone and I used to listen to these white fellas play, white boys play. And they had a style that they got actually a C melody sound on an alto saxophone. And didn't use a style that required a lot of choice notes. They used a rolling profuse style with a lot of notes. And actually it was a tenor style with a C melody sound. There was a fellow in town that used to be proficient at that, Steve Massey Coat. I don't know what he's doing, if he's dead alive now. And he is my, he's what I'd call my idea, or I would typify the New Orleans style of jazz saxophone. And that always, always interests me. And when I go to different cities and they listen to different styles, or run across different musicians, nobody quite captured that style. But the Negro musician in New Orleans, he doesn't have much of a style on saxophone, and he doesn't use it too much.
No, that's true. He doesn't use it. What about, did you think there was any difference in the rhythm sections between colored and white?

Yeah, contrary to a lot of, to many people's opinion, we call it two beat, two four Dixieland music. It's associated with that. And the thing that surprised me the most is that these guys, for the most part, lay down a heavy four beat rhythm, you see. Just a punching style, you know, just a pounding style. And one of the few, a few musicians that I work with, I got to know very well, that had a light two beat style was Ray Badouk, Monk Hazel, you see. But for the most part, take Paul Barberin, you know, he laid down the hardest four beat driving style, and it would just pound right ahead like a herd of elephants, you see. And so did most of these drummers that played for us. Of course, Freddie Coleman is relatively a new drummer. He worked here a couple of years for us. We made a few record albums together. He's primarily a big band drummer, and he's more of the modern school, but he's capable of playing any style, any style of drum. But the rhythm section did amaze me. When Celestan was in here, let's see, who was on banjo for Celestan? Is that guy probably French? Must have been, yeah.
The guy that calls himself now probably French, I can't remember. He's the leader of the band, which has called itself the Celestan Band. I'm not sure whether he was playing for them then, maybe.

I don't know. I'd have to look up some pictures. We managed to keep some pictures, which I should have taken more of, because, believe me, they're treasured. And, uh, Celestan would be up there playing with these high, high-button shoes, and, uh, the band would be just driving. It sounded like a herd of elephants going down the street with a banjo and the piano playing four. Four, now, no two-beat on the piano rhythm, but just a straight-four drive, you know? And it had a tremendous, exciting effect. And it was a little bogey and a little heavy, and it wasn't a light thing, you know, sort of being a light thing. But it was a savage drive, a pounding drive, you know? And that's the first thing that, uh, I said, I wonder what happened to the two-beat light Dixieland? Like, .
Yeah. And I agree, I think it did get too heavy. Yes, it did. And what did you think about George's, George's own playing as a clarinet player? What did you think?

George had a wealth of ideas. He had a wealth of ideas. None of these, uh, not just George, but none of these colored musicians. Two schools. They're not two schools. They, they didn't make any great study of their horn. And I had a clarinet player, I can't recall his name, that worked here on an off night with a band for me. And I told him one time he had to tune his clarinet because he was terribly sharp, you know? And he said, you can't tune a clarinet, Mr. Sid, you see? And I said, you're mistaken that with an oboe or something else, you see? But you can tune a clarinet. And I showed him how to do it. And I think he had played 30, 35 years and he never bothered to tune that clarinet. He would try to lip it, whether sharp or flat, he'd try to lip it into tune, you see? So actually not too many of them were proficient. That wasn't George, really.

No, indeed it wasn't George. Because George sometimes did have a tendency to play a little sharp, you know? Yeah, it wasn't George. Especially if he had a piano. So he, um... What did you think of George's tone?

George had a good sound and most of them get a... Most colored musicians I find are not at their best on the clarinet because they'll get an anti-vibrata, an awfully fast vibrata. And a thin tone, more or less. And I found George was George's clarinet and for the old time, I guess we can call him that, New Orleans musician was probably more pleasing than anyone I've heard about him. He had a wealth of good ideas. He, uh, had a pretty fair command of his instrument. He was no master of the clarinet, but he would get those hands and find those notes some kind of way. Yeah. Whereas if he had a better study of the clarinet, had had a better study of the clarinet, he would have known the different figurines that he could substitute, you know? Yeah. Because I used to watch him. But, uh, George's a beautiful clarinet man. Beautiful man. But he did have a name of a brighter.
And I find that, uh, it's a lot. What do you call it? A what vibrata?

Nanny vibrata. Nanny. It's a little, uh, whether vibrata is a little too, uh, exaggerated or too fast, you see. Because it should be controlled. But, uh, many of them have that, whether it's trumpet or trombone or, uh, or clarinet.
Did you have lessons yourself, musical lessons?

Yes, I studied pretty, uh, pretty much. And, uh, then I attended the New Orleans Conservatory, which is affiliated, I believe, now with, uh, Loyola School of Music. But at the time it was called the New Orleans Conservatory. Uh, Dr. Skyton was ahead of it. And, uh, we had the New Orleans Symphony, I played bassoon in the New Orleans Symphony. And what I did was try to... You tried what? Bassoon.
Oh, really?

What I tried to do was to, uh, make a thorough study of music. I wasn't too particularly interested in jazz. I wanted to be a classical musician. When I was about fifteen or sixteen, I had a radio program on WWL. Once or twice a week, and I'd play, uh, saxophone solos, just for the piano, you see. The technical things, and Rudy Weedhoff, and all that stuff, Andy Sonniler, and that. And Al Gallador and I became friends, and he's a very proficient musician, and a master of his own. That's one of the times they had Vortville in the theaters. He played in the theater, called the Offium. And there were good bands in the theaters before the talking pictures came in, you see. But, uh, it was a lot easier, I guess, to make a living playing popular music and jazz than it was classical music. But anyway, I fell into it some kind of way, and, uh, and I found that I enjoyed it, and I guess I stayed with it.
Tell me now about your uncle.

Oh, my Uncle Joe. Yeah, he was a killer. He wrote some songs around the turn of the century. Uh, yeah, he used to have some copies somewhere. I remember, in particular one time, they'd write up in a newspaper about him. He, um, around the turn of the century, around the first war, something like that. There was a series of murders in New Orleans. And these people were bludgeoning to death with an axe. Uh, and he wrote a song called The Axe Man Blooms. I don't know where he got the title from, because I don't know who would buy the song. But, uh, and at the time they used to sing the sheet music at the dime stores in town. That's how they would hawk it, you know. You'd go down and you'd ask Dave Frank or somebody, a fellow named Frank Arena, there'd be a lady piano player sitting in the McCrory's, uh, Woolworths, and you'd say, would you play this for me? And sheet music was a big thing in those days, because everybody played a little piano at home. And they'd sing a chorus for you, really, and whether you liked it or not, I mean, if you like it, you'd buy it. And, uh, Uncle Joe wrote, uh, well, quite a few tunes. I just don't recall many of them, but, uh, and he was acquainted with a lot of musicians, you know. Did you know him?
You remember him?

Yeah, he died about, uh, he died about, uh, ten, twelve years ago. He was no, uh, uh, no versatile musician, but he'd played the piano by ear, and he could manage to put a few notes down on paper, you see. But he, uh, I guess he had written and recorded many, many songs. Uh, Gene Austin recorded some of his songs, and, uh, the sister trio that came out of New Orleans, the Basel Sisters, you know, they're from New Orleans. As a matter of fact, he managed them for a while. But I didn't have any association with him, I mean, uh, as the music went, because, uh, I didn't know about him too well, or, too much, and, uh, except that he used to come pop a bunch of sheet music on my sister's piano every now and then, you know. Mother's the only one I care for now, and, uh, stuff like that. I said, where'd these old songs come from? I just wondered if my sister kept some of them.
Did you have any other music in your family at all?

Not that I recall. I had a, uh, grandfather, I think it was, played in the Paris Symphony, cello. That's all I can, uh, that's all I can, uh, that's all I can find. That's all I've been able to, you know, determine. My people are from, uh, some are from, uh, Portugal. And, uh, my mother's people are from France. And, uh, it's a little hard. Not too many of them are over here.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.

I thought there was as much of that type music or that style of music played everywhere else. And it wasn't some time later that we found out that this was where the thing started from and what do we call it, the cradle of jazz. And most styles, and this style evolved from New Orleans and was carried up north by some musicians, you know. But no, I wasn't conscious of that. I just thought everybody should do it that way and everybody did it that way. You'd see a guy, and what it raised me when I first began to play music, I'd speak with some musicians somewhere, find out that they couldn't read music. And how do you play so well? How do you do it, you see? I guess I don't have the greatest ear in the world because, or else I started on the wrong hand. These guys, a lot of these guys started reading music, such as myself. Some guys just picked up the horn and started playing it, you know. Now Raymond Burke would give me an argument every time, you know. Raymond, I said, well, you don't read music at all? And he said, no. And I'd say, well, it would kind of open, I think they would kind of broaden your feeling and broaden your horizon a little bit if you could read, even sparingly, even hulkily. He said, that would interfere with my improvisation. He said, I refuse to learn how to read music. And Harry Shields was of that, too. Harry Shields would do that all the time. You see, we had Sharky in here. Sharky worked for us a while with Harry Shields, George Brunis, and Jake Martin. And Harry would give you that argument. He thought that if he learned to read any music, it would be more of a hindrance and it would be a help. And perhaps so, because, but perhaps not. Perhaps not. Mike broadened his understanding of harmony. Yeah. Broadened his scope of harmony.

Very difficult to say, some of those guys who were, or like Bunk Johnson, for instance, was a trumpet player. He could read music. He was a good reader. And others, you see, like George Lewis could never read music.
Not even haltingly?
No, he'd never, he'd never learned to read music at all. He didn't seem to make too much difference. So I guess there's no real rules about it.

I don't think so, no. I like to believe that it would broaden, if you broaden your knowledge about what you're doing in some sense, that the feel might become larger and you could feel more free to move around harmonically, you know. But then again, too, if you start thinking about what you're doing, sometimes you don't do it as well, you know.
Yeah, so I'm exactly right.
I think it's a good thing, particularly a thing that you should do naturally, and essentially just playing music, I guess. You either got a feel for it or you don't have.
What do you think now about the future of this music now? I don't know. Dix-Land. Oh, Dix-Land.
Oh, Dix-Land.
Oh, yeah.

Well, Dix-Land never has died, of course, very well. And, but it has seasons of popularity. It got to be the end thing to do, you know, whether or not, how many times these people would come in with the mink coat. And I didn't know a bass drum from a cannon, but sometimes it sounded like. But we'd come in here and it was a thing to do, it was to go to dinner at Antwine's or Brennan's and we'll listen to some Dix-Land. And then you tell your social life friends, I went down and I heard some Dix-Land. It was a thing to do, it was a fashionable thing to do, and it rolled along for many years like that because of that, not completely because of that altogether, but because that played a big part of it. Which wasn't a bad thing to subject these people to some music, you know, well, good gracious. And, but they didn't know what they were listening to, most of them, but again and again, but then again, there were the people that did know. But for the most part, it was a fashionable thing to do, it was like, so you get a little television exposure, we must go down and see you. Whether we appreciate really or know really what you're putting down, we must go see you because we saw you on television.
Do you think that that, do you think that that has changed now?

That's not so much the end thing to do anymore, I don't know, it's, um, well, uh, I guess it's not, it's not as fast, well, it's fast, but let me get away from that, it's not as popular as it was, let's put it that way. Because after dinner on the street, these little three jazz places would be jam-packed, you just couldn't get in there. People would come in for their drink and clap their hands and stomp their feet a little while and listen to some music and then they'd go home. But they'd do it again next week and the next week and I'd see the same people on a Friday and Saturday and just like clockwork. But now it's, they've gotten away from that a little bit. But everything must change and it's a gradual process.

Of course these places like Preservation Hall, they pack in big crowds. They, uh, I understand that. Or is that a different kind of, do you think that's a different kind of an audience, I guess, than the audience you've got?

I don't know too much about them, Tom, but I do believe that some of the regular, some of the die-hard Vixeland fans do frequent those places. But then too, I think that just a lot of visitors drop in. And whether, what degree, what varying degrees they like music, whether it's just curiosity many times. But since Dixieland and some of these musicians have gotten so much international publicity and, uh, not too much lately perhaps, but about eight, ten years, twelve years ago, you know, they were going to Japan and Schocker wanted me to go to Japan with him and bing,
ding, ding, ringy ding.

I had a son incidentally, a pilot in the Air Force was stationed at Tachikawa near Japan. And who do you think, he walked in the officers club and they came back and they brought me all kinds of things. And who do you think, including some programs, he walks in the officers club and he says, who do I see in there? I see George Lewis, I see Bill Robichaud, the whole smear from the Mardi Gras Lounge, you know, in here. He was, George was out there for him. Yeah.
He had his big success of him, about three years, three success of him, tours. Oh, they loved him. They loved him. They loved him.

Now they, a number of New Orleans musicians have made Japan their home, you know. Matter of fact, I had a few tempting offers to go over there, teach in the schools and play music. And like the money was adequate, you know. Matter of fact, there's a friend of mine over there, there are two Costa boys in town who have been musicians for years. One is Tony Costa and one is Mike Costa. Excellent musicians. What do you think now about the future of Bourbon Street in general? What do you think there? I mean, it's of course changing all the time. Do you think, do you see any particular direction in which it's going to be going to be

changing? For instance, like these new motels, hotels they're building here, they've got three new ones in the last few years. I don't know what's going to happen to Bourbon Street, Tom, because it's been a busy street, and it's a lot busier on the outside than it is on the inside, actually, when you read the register in the morning. That's true.

But it has attracted a lot of attention and a lot of investment people. In the next block, in the next block, there are two dress shops, and there will be another restaurant going up. And there will be another restaurant going up. Instant food, fast food, and propositions. And on orange juice concern, nationally known, they've opened up down the street, and they wanted to lease this place for me to put an orange juice stand. People are selling canned beans, hot water, and bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo In the next block, in the next block, there are two dress shops, and there will be another restaurant going up with instant food, fast food propositions. And on orange juice concern, nationally known, they've opened up down the street and they wanted to lease this place for me to put an orange juice stand in. They were selling canned beans, hot sandwiches out the window, to see what else is going in. And there's some dress shops up in the 200 block, and novelty shops, souvenir shops. So actually, people try to get on what they think is a bandwagon. You must go where people ought to make a buck. But what does bring the people down on the street, they like to look in the doors, see the girls on the stage, stand outside and listen to the music. And that's what's been a big factor. I had a talk with Ronnie Cole last week, and there's some way we could block off Bourbon Street and charge so much to get on the street, you know, because I think they do that in Coney Island. They get on the midway at 50 Cent's. And charge you so much to get on the street, because if you're going to walk outside the door and listen to the music and look in the door, then we'll all put this money in a kitty in a common cause and split it up at the end of the month and help us with our salaries.
Well, I know what you mean. I agree with you that it is definitely busier on the outside than the inside. Do you think this is a recent trend?

More so, more so recently. Before because of, it's a curiosity and it's a, a few places in the nation where all the nightclub entertainment or just about virtually all of it is compressed into a few blocks. And it's, uh, occupies, now there's nothing on the side streets from out to anything anymore. It's just Bourbon Street, which they call the strip. Just Bourbon Street from about, there's nothing in the 200 block, 100 block, 200 block to about the 700 block, about six blocks. And that's it. You can walk in a dozen times a night, you see, and look in the doors and feel the excitement and sense, uh, uh, hey, I'm having a ball, I'm living it up, you know? And not fair penny. And not fair penny. And not fair penny. If you get thirsty, you can get a beer for 35 cents out of some window, or a highball, or a sandwich. So consequently, they're in the, they're in the, uh, majority now. They're the lookers and the walkers. So I guess that's the reason for the dearth of some of these clubs there. They're, uh, folding or changing their policy or something, you see.
The number of strip clubs on Bourbon Street diminished?

Yes, yes. Yes, greatly. From 16, I think there's nine, uh, there's about nine left. I, uh, been torn with the idea of picking my horn up for so long and, uh, putting the jazz on back in here, which I'm gonna do ultimately. I bet you I'm gonna do it. But after that little, uh, after that little, uh, escapade I had with Bill Matthews there for six weeks, cost me about $3,000. $54,000. And I don't have the kind of money to gamble, you know, or two months like that. I have to kind of play close to my chest. Yeah.
Sure it would be. It would be a gamble. Yeah.
But I know we, uh, we packed them in before, and, uh, packed them in. I don't know if we could do again.
How long is it since you played? Oh, about eight, nine years. Really?
I never meant to, uh, abandon it, you know, Tom. I just, tomorrow I'll pick it up.
Tomorrow I'll pick it up.

And tomorrow never came. And the only thing I was taught with now is, uh, teaching my daughter piano, and I'll just play some piano for a while, you know, occasionally. But then again, music kind of went out of style, didn't it? Oh, and I think I picked a good time to get away from it. Because everything was rock and roll, and what we call the rock now. And it's been in the way for a long, ten years. Yeah.

About ten years. Well, that, they've got this, you know, this very large stuff, like they have, is it that way or that way? That way. That way. That way, puppies, yes. That's the latest, uh, thing that everybody thinks today.

Well, it's on its way out now. I understand the biggest discotheque in, uh, New York called Arthur. They're for sale. And these things are dying on the street. There aren't too many of them left anyway, thank God, because with that, uh, amplification was too much. Too much. I mean, they weren't content with you hearing the music. They had to, you know, just actually beat your eardrums in with it. I don't know how they stand it. But it's on its way out. Now the thing seems to be too a little, uh, the folk has gone somewhat waned in popularity. Now it's the rhythm and blues thing that's come back. What we did was Smiling Joe up there, and Joe Robichaud and Lizzie Miles and Blanche Thomas did up there. But we always did the blues for New Orleans and rhythm and blues. And Joe was another one that should have gone ahead and made himself a million dollars, because he is one of the most talented bluesmen, you know. Do you know Smiling Joe? Yes, I know.
He used to play the guitar.
Now he's just fooling with the piano a little bit.
Yeah, he plays up there on the 600 blocks.

And he's just, uh, great. Yes, great. But that seems to be the thing now I see with, uh, for popularity. So we're getting back to, it's not folk music and it's not completely blues, but it is a, I believe it's sort of a combination of folk, rhythm, and blues. The style that's evolving now, or gelling, you know, which would be popular for a while. And I hate to think what the next one will be, I don't know. But Lizzy was here, Lizzy Miles, she, um, I met Lizzy on a radio interview. Tony Almericka used to have a band in town, and, uh, he was a disc jockey. So, uh, we played Dixieland music and he was a big advocate of Dixieland jazz. And we had a place called, uh, Parisian Room, and he had jazz concerts on a Sunday afternoon. And he was one of the guys actually, uh, instrumental in the big Dixieland revival because, and then he got a line up for nationwide broadcast right from there, you see. And Fazola, probably the world's greatest blues clarinet player, had come to town and Fazola was playing with him. And, uh, so he got a little, uh, radio program and, uh, uh, I was up for an interview with Shawke and some other guys one day. And I met Lizzy Miles, who used to continually write letters to Tony Almericka about his misinformation. You got the years wrong. It wasn't 1927 and it wasn't Bessie Smith. So I happened to be up there one day and here comes Lizzy Miles, dressed 1924 style, with a parlor record set. Well, believe me, it must have been worth a hundred dollars a piece collector's items. And Lizzy set him straight and we got to talking over there. And, uh, I felt that Lizzy should be on before the people. She wasn't singing. She was a washerwoman. She had gotten out of her business fifteen to twenty years. And, uh, we put Lizzy on the street with a piano player, on the stage with a piano player. And she began singing these songs, many songs in French. And Lizzy went on to make a lot of records and make some good appearances. She did national television, NBC, I think, national television. She played some of the bigger clubs in the country. And she always came back here because she was a religious woman and she had taken some kind of a vow many years ago that she wouldn't appear on the stage if something were granted her. So she, uh, she made a distinction between a bandstand and a stage and she got up there easy. And she was a little bit of a band. But she was a wonderful one.
What about the El Moraco? That was the place where they used to have some, um, George used to play there.
George played at the El Moraco many, many, many years ago.
I don't know for how long. He was at the El Moraco.

And what other bands they had, I don't know, but, uh, I see they were, they wind up with girl shows and, uh, with this crusading discraternity that looked down his nose on girl shows and girl activities. They were closed up. And, uh, so they didn't have a real girl shows or Dixieland either. But they did a year ago, I'm sorry, a year ago. They had a little group from England, I believe. Right. You were acquainted with them? No, I wasn't playing. I went down there and I didn't know.
Yeah. And they stayed there a while and then they drifted away where to, I don't know.
I think some of them went back to England.
I can see just from seeing that, it's difficult for them, for anybody to make it to that kind of music, because I know they didn't really have any big business down there.

No, it's a difficult thing, I mean, what you'd like to have and what you can afford, I guess, to see, uh, whether it's, uh, trying to run a nightclub with entertainment or, uh, buying an automobile, I guess you've got to do what you can afford to do. Of course, we tried, we tried, and we, uh, we were so happy with it. It was a wonderful sight to walk in this place and see some, uh, genuinely happy people looking up and seeing some faces on the stage, like, uh, George Lewis, Papa Selesdan, Joe Robichaud, uh, oh, name them. And incidentally, I was the first guy to put, sounds like this and there for me, first guy to put Sweet Emma back on the street. Oh, yeah. And we talked and put in the garters on and she was kind of reluctant about the garter. And the grand piano was over there in the corner and, uh, I put a little light shining on her legs so people would know where that sound was coming from, because we got tired of people asking us, who, who's playing the bells? You know, who's playing the bells? Yeah, it wouldn't be sweet, Emma.
She became quite a hit, right? Mm-hmm. Yeah. Well, I think that's about it with just about attitude.
I guess I've digressed. I didn't know exactly what you wanted to do.
Well, that's fine.
Well, I can tell you about some things, I can tell you a lot about some things, and so little about some other things. Well, that's fine. That's just really about it.
Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .

segments.title: Interview opening at the Mardi Gras Lounge
segments.summary: Date, place and confirmation of the club's name.

segments.title: Opening the club to play Dixieland, August 1951
segments.summary: Sid wanted to be his own boss and play the music he liked; the club became the third Dixieland room on Bourbon Street.

segments.chapter: George Lewis and the house bands
segments.title: Hiring George Lewis and hearing him first
segments.summary: Bands were rotated; Papa Celestin's last steady job was here. Sid first heard George Lewis on records and at the Patek Lounge, then hired him twice for months.

segments.chapter: George Lewis and the house bands
segments.title: Six-night schedule, Lizzie Miles and Kid Howard
segments.summary: Weekly schedule, Lizzie Miles filling in with Joe Robichaux, and a band built for Kid Howard.

segments.chapter: George Lewis and the house bands
segments.title: Nightly sets, repertoire and packed crowds
segments.summary: How the sets ran, authentic Dixieland only, and crowds too big for the room.

segments.chapter: George Lewis and the house bands
segments.title: Sitting in, and identifying a George Lewis band photo
segments.summary: Sid sat in with the band; they look at a photo of Lawrence Marrero, Percy Humphrey, Slow Drag and Jim Robinson.

segments.title: Bourbon Street's change into a midway
segments.summary: Strip clubs, three jazz places, and the shift to restaurants and concert-style jazz halls.

segments.title: First Dixieland on Bourbon Street, Leon Prima's 500 Club
segments.summary: Dixieland for dancing at the 500 Club c. 1947-48; before the war the street played pop and modern styles.

segments.title: Replacing the band with girl shows over a tax bind
segments.summary: A tax bind forced a quick choice; Sid put in strippers, which he regrets.

segments.title: Street control rumours and the 1963 attempt to bring a band back
segments.summary: Places are individually owned; Sid tried Bill Matthews' band in 1963.

segments.title: The Famous Door, the Paddock and bus tours
segments.summary: Rival clubs, their music, and how bus tours keep a few places alive.

segments.title: Starting music at twelve and early teachers
segments.summary: Sid began around 1928, absorbing New Orleans jazz, then studied saxophone and clarinet with Jean Parquet and Tony Parenti.

segments.title: Gentilly childhood, Louis Armstrong on radio, parades
segments.summary: House-party bands, hearing Armstrong broadcast from Suburban Gardens, and Mardi Gras parades.

segments.title: White and Black Dixieland saxophone styles
segments.summary: The rolling C-melody-like New Orleans white saxophone style versus Black players.

segments.title: Two-beat versus four-beat rhythm sections
segments.summary: Heavy four-beat drumming, Celestin's band, and the lost light two-beat style.

segments.title: George Lewis's clarinet playing, tone and vibrato
segments.summary: Sid's view of George Lewis's ideas, tone and limited study, plus clarinet tuning.

segments.title: Conservatory studies, bassoon and early radio work
segments.summary: Sid studied at the New Orleans Conservatory, played bassoon, aimed for classical music, and had a WWL radio program.

segments.title: Uncle Joe the songwriter and family background
segments.summary: Uncle Joe wrote songs including the Axe Man piece; a grandfather played cello; family from Portugal and France.

segments.title: Reading music versus playing by ear
segments.summary: Raymond Burke, Harry Shields and George Lewis did not read; the cradle of jazz was not apparent to Sid.

segments.title: Dixieland as a fashionable fad and its decline
segments.summary: Dixieland had seasons of popularity; society crowds came for fashion, now less so.

segments.title: Preservation Hall, Japan tours and musicians abroad
segments.summary: Sid's son saw George Lewis's band in Japan; musicians moved to Japan.

segments.title: Bourbon Street's future: new shops, lookers and walkers
segments.summary: New restaurants and shops; crowds watch from outside; Sid's idea of a street admission.

segments.chapter: Later years and the club's fate
segments.title: Thoughts of bringing jazz back; Sid has stopped playing
segments.summary: Fewer strip clubs, cost of the Matthews attempt, and Sid has not played for about nine years.

segments.title: Rock, rhythm and blues and Smiling Joe
segments.summary: Rock fading, rhythm and blues returning, and Joe Robichaux's talent.

segments.chapter: Later years and the club's fate
segments.title: Meeting Lizzie Miles and bringing her to the club
segments.summary: How Sid met Lizzie Miles through a radio interview and put her on stage; her career afterwards.

segments.chapter: Later years and the club's fate
segments.title: The El Moraco and a visiting English group
segments.summary: George Lewis once played the El Moraco; later a group from England played there.

segments.chapter: Later years and the club's fate
segments.title: Memories of the bands, Sweet Emma, and closing
segments.summary: Happy memories of Lewis, Celestin and Robichaux, bringing Sweet Emma back, and wrapping up.
